Headline: 3 held for siphoning off money from ATMs
Full Content:
KATHMANDU, MAR 26 -
Nepal Police on Sunday arrested three Indian nationals from Mahendranagar, Kanchanpur, for withdrawing cash illegally from ATM s using fake debit cards.
A team of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CIB) on Monday brought the arrestees to Kathmandu for further investigation. The police said the arrested trio withdrew cash using fake Nepal Investment Bank Limited (NIBL) debit cards. As more than two dozen ATM cards of both Nepali and Indian banks were seized from the detainees, the police suspect they might have withdrawn cash from other banks as well.
The police, however, did not disclose the names of the arrested individuals as doing so may give leeway to others involved in the case to escape.
NIBL confirmed the cash withdrawal, but said it did not cause a major loss to the bank. A senior NIBL official said the individuals withdrew around 150,000 from the bank. “As they were arrested before they could withdraw more money, there has not been any problem with other accounts and debit cards,” the official said.
After the incident, the bank has imposed an ATM withdrawal limit of Rs 5,000 a day. “We will continue this provision probably for a few more days until the problem is resolved,” said a bank source.
The bank termed the incident ‘data compromise’, which means the racketeers were able to gain access to the bank’s clients’ data. “We are investigating on how they got access to the clients’ data. For this, we have taken help from the risk analysis team of Visa,” said another NIBL official.
After a customer last week complained that his money was withdrawn from India without his knowledge, the bank had started monitoring the cards being used in India, the source said. “About 1,000 cards are used in India daily,” said the source. “After the monitoring, we disqualified 35 of them.”
After finding that attempts were being made to withdraw cash even using the disqualified cards, the bank informed the police. “We tracked them by limiting the amount they could withdraw and informed the police,” the source added.
The bank said the individuals frequently withdrew money from Mahendranagar as well as from bordering Indian towns, which raised suspicion.
Of late, incidents of fraud through the use fake ATM cards are increasing. “Such incidents have taught us that we have to be more alert to ensure security of the card system,” said Rajan Singh Bhandari, president of Nepal Bankers’ Association. He said such incidents are taking place due to ill intention of a few individuals.
Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) officials, however, say the banks have deficiencies in managing operational risks. “We have found several cases in which a single person has been given access to the clients’ data,” said a senior NRB official.
“The banks should have a clear risk management plan about how much access to the clients’ data should be given to a single person.”
Given the central bank already issuing information technology guideline and directing banks to conduct system audit, NRB officials said the banks should follow the directions and the guidelines properly to avoid operational risks. “We are looking into possible operational risks during supervision and we have also increased the amount of capital charge for operational risks from 2 to 5 percent of the gross income made in the previous year,” said the NRB official.
Source: The Kathmandu Post

The bank that has a paid up capital of more than Rs 3.76 billion — including proposed bonus shares — from its initial paid up capital of Rs 30 million is one the leading banks in the country, he said, adding it has the highest paid up capital among private sector banks in the country and is almost twice the minimum paid up capital prescribed by NRB. “It has also strengthened foundation and credibility of NIBL.”
The last fiscal year 2011-12 was yet another challenging year for the bank and the banking industry as a whole, he said, adding that the bank was able to post satisfactory results despite the challenges.
The bank’s total assets, deposits and lending increased by 12.7 per cent, 13.7 per cent and 2.4 per cent to Rs 65.75 billion, Rs 57.01 billion and Rs 42.90 billion, respectively.
Likewise, it posted a robust growth of 40.6 per cent to reach Rs 10.64 billion in total investments. However, owing to
surplus liquidity
in the market, returns on investments are very low which have adversely affected the bank’s interest income, Pandey added. “Despite a fall in net interest income by Rs 14.8 million (Rs 2.16 billion against Rs 2.18 billion a year back), the operating profit before provision posted a growth of Rs 49.8 million, mainly due to an increase in fee based and exchange income and tight control on overheads.”
However, due to the increase in loan loss provision on real estate loans, net profit declined by 11.7 per cent to Rs 1.03 billion against Rs 1.17 billion last year, he added. The capital adequacy ratio (CAR) and
credit deposit ratio
(LCY deposit with equity) are maintained at comfortable levels of 11.1 per cent and 72.4 per cent.
The central bank has asked banks to maintain a minimum CAR of 10 per cent and CD ratio — LCY deposit with equity — of not more than 80 per cent. “Our returns on paid up capital and return on shareholders’ fund stand at 34.5 per cent and 20.1 per cent, respectively,” Pandey said, adding that the market share in deposits and lending stands at 6.6 per cent and seven per cent, respectively.
Chairman of the bank Prithivi Bahadur Pandé, who was also the CEO of the bank, resigned from the post of CEO on July 16, and Jyoti Prakash Pandey, who was GM, was appointed as CEO by the board.
Rated Nepal (A) for the third consecutive year by Indian Credit Rating Agency, an affiliate of Moody’s Investor Group, the bank has a branch network of 41 and one extension counter along with 68 ATMs.

Headline: ICRA gives Nepal Investment Bank Ltd. (A) tag
Full Content:
KATHMANDU, FEB 19:
Nepal Investment Bank Ltd (NIBL) has retained the rating of (Nepal) A from the Indian Credit Rating Agency (ICRA), an associate of Moody’s Investors Service.
The rating for issuers in Nepal is assigned on a scale, which ranges from (Nepal) AAA to (Nepal) D, according to the bank. The rating of NIBL factors in the bank’s good market position in Nepal, adequate earning profile, and its experienced management team, it said, adding that the real estate portfolio has been mitigated by adequate security coverage norms of the bank.
ICRA has also noted with concern the tight liquidity condition in Nepal, though the liquidity profile has improved over the last few months. NIBL’s comfortable liquidity profile even during the tight liquidity conditions indicate strength, according to ICRA.
The bank — one of the largest private sector banks in Nepal — has been able to maintain a comfortable profitability profile largely led by adequate net interest margins and control on credit provisions as its capitalisation levels are adequate (CRAR of 11.11 per cent as on mid-Jan-2012).
“It had lower credit growth in 2010-11 and intends to maintain a lower growth in the short to medium term,” added the bank that has 41 branches and 67 ATMs.
As of mid-July 2011, NIBL had a market share of about seven per cent in terms of deposit base and total advances of the banking system in Nepal.
It reported a net profit of Rs 1.17 billion in fiscal year 2010-11 over an asset base of Rs 57.36 billion as of mid-July 2011, compared to a net profit of Rs 1.26 billion over an asset base of Rs 58.3 billion as of mid-July 2010.

Headline: US bank stalls NIBL payment through Iran
Full Content:
KATHMANDU, FEB 18 -
The US sanctions on Iran have resulted in a payment for bitumen imported to Nepal from Dubai stalling for the last one year.
The payment had to go from Nepal Investment Bank Limited’s (NIBL) account with a US bank to an Iranian bank, which in turn should have paid the bitumen exporter.
Nepal’s Vinira Holding, a bitumen importer, failed to make a payment of $20,000 to its Dubai-based exporter, Bridge Oil Industry, as the City Bank in the US refused to transfer the amount after it came to know that the payment should go through an Iranian bank.
The importer had opened a letter of credit (LC) at the NIBL for the import.
The amount, equivalent of that to be transferred, was also deducted from the NIBL account in the City Bank’s New York branch.
“As the amount to be paid to the exporting party had to be transferred through an Iranian bank, City Bank refused to make the transfer,” said Rajan Amatya, a deputy general manager of NIBL.
According to Amatya, the importer not mentioning the name of the Iranian bank while filling up the LC form resulted in the deduction of the amount from the NIBL’s City Bank account.
“The importer, Rit Gupta, had simply used the swift code of the Iranian bank, which was not identified here and the LC, too, was treated as other normal LCs,” Amatya said. “We would not have tried to make the payment through the US if it was known earlier that it should go through an Iranian Bank.”
If a payment is to be made to Iran, it is done through the Asian Currency Unit (ACU) dollar mechanism. Through the ACU mechanism, dollars deposited in various Asian financial centres are paid to parties concerned.
NIBL said it is trying to get back the amount, both through the US Embassy here and its correspondence bank in the US. It has also requested the Nepal Rastra Bank to help solve the problem.
A senior NRB official said the central bank inquired about a possible solution to the problem with officials of the US Embassy. “They told us that they could take steps to have the cash refunded, but that the amount cannot be transferred to the beneficiary party in Dubai,” the NRB official said.
The central bank has also asked the Finance Ministry to do the needful in solving the problem diplomatically.
Source: Kantipur

Headline: Shareholders urge NIBL to go for merger
Full Content:
KATHMANDU, NOV 12:
The shareholders of Nepal Investment Bank Ltd (NIBL) suggested the management to opt for merger with a viable partner in order to retain its position as market leader in the bank’s Annual General Meeting (AGM) conducted today.
“The merger with other banks are under consideration as that will be more cost-effective measure for the bank to achieve better performance in the increased competitive environment,” said Prithivi Bahadur Pande, chairman Of NIBL.
The AGM also approved the distribution of distributing 25 per cent cash dividend and 25 per cent bonus share to its shareholders from its profit of Rs 1.17 billion in the last fiscal year.
After releasing 25 per cent bonus share, NIBL will be the only private commercial bank to have paid up capital of over Rs 3 billion. NIBL also has the largest asset base of any private bank at Rs. 59.10 billion. The bank that completed its 25th years in operation this February is one of the largest private commercial banks in Nepal at present.
NIBL serves more than 425,000 customers through its 41 branches and 67 ATMs throughout the country.
The bank was established as a joint venture bank –Nepal Indosuez Bank Ltd in 1986 between Indosuez Bank, Rastriya Banijya Bank, Rastriya Beema Sansthan and public stakeholders. After French banking group –Credit Agricole took over Indosuez Bank Group in 2002 then the French party sold its stake in the bank to a Nepali group who re-branded the bank as Nepal Investment Bank.
The bank has donated Rs 500,000 to Shiva Parbati Briddashram, one of the oldest old age homes in Nepal. NIBL contributed Rs 200,000 to Hospital and Rehabilitation Center for Disabled Children (HRDC). The bank sponsored over Rs 100,000 to Kasthamandap Vidyalaya, in last one year.
